Surah al-Shams (The Sun)
Fifteen verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sun and its brightness,﴾ ﴿and by the moon when it follows it.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿By the sun and its brightness,﴾ ﴿and by the moon when it follows it.﴾ Before beginning the exegesis (tafsir), some issues must be addressed:

The first issue: The purpose of this surah is to encourage obedience and warn against disobedience.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, constantly draws His servants' attention by swearing by various kinds of His creations that contain great benefits, so that the responsible person (mukallaf) will reflect upon them and give thanks for them. This is because that by which Allah swears produces an impression upon the heart, so the motives to reflect upon it become stronger.

The second issue: You know that a group of the scholars of the foundational sciences (ahl al-usul) said: the implied phrase is "and the Lord of the sun, and the Lord of the rest of what He mentioned," up to the end of the oath. Others argued against these views, saying: within this oath is His saying ﴿and the sky and what built it﴾, and that refers to Allah, exalted is He, so it would follow that the intended meaning is "and the Lord of the sky and its Lord," which is almost self-contradictory. Al-Qadi (al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar) answered this by saying that His saying ﴿and what built it﴾ cannot mean Allah, exalted is He, because "ma" (what) is not used for the Creator of the sky except in a kind of metaphorical usage; and because it is not permissible for Him to place an oath by something else before His oath by Himself; and because He, exalted is He, is hardly ever mentioned together with others in this manner. Therefore, an interpretation is necessary, namely that "ma" together with what follows it has the force of a verbal noun (maṣdar), so the implied meaning is: "and the sky and its building." The author of the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) objected to this, saying: if the matter were in this way, it would follow from the conjunction of His saying ﴿then inspired it﴾ to it a corruption of the composition.

The third issue: The readers (qurra') differ regarding the endings (fawasil) of this surah and similar ones, such as ﴿by the night when it covers﴾, ﴿by the forenoon﴾, and ﴿by the night when it is still﴾. They recited them at times with imala (inclining the alif toward the ya' sound), at times with tafkhim (emphatic, full pronunciation), and at times some of them with imala and some with tafkhim.

[Page 172]
Al-Farra' said: "With the kasra in ḍuḥāhā (the vowel is) i." The verses that follow it, even though the original of some of them is a waw, such as talāhā, taḥāhā and daḥāhā, are likewise. Since the surah began with a letter of ya', it followed it with what derives from waw, because the alif that changed from waw may coincide with the alif that changed from ya'. Do you not see that talawtu, taḥawtu and similar forms may, in their verbs, change into ya', such as talī and daḥī? When this correspondence occurred, they permitted inclining it, just as they permitted inclining what originated from ya'.

As for the view of those who abandoned imala entirely, it is that many of the Arabs do not incline these alifs, nor do they lean them toward the ya' sound. What strengthens leaving the alif unaltered is that the waw in mūsar is changed from ya', and the ya' in mīqāt and mīzān is changed from waw, yet this did not require that something appear in it indicating that change. Therefore, here too the alif should be left uninclined and not leaned toward the ya' sound.

As for inclining some and not inclining others, as Hamzah did, this is also good, because the alif is only inclined toward ya' in order to indicate ya' when its change is from ya'. In talāhā, taḥāhā and daḥāhā there is no alif changed from ya'; rather, it is changed from waw, as shown by talawtu and daḥawtu.

The fourth issue: Allah, exalted is He, swore by seven things up to His saying ﴿has succeeded﴾, and that is the response to the oath. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "indeed he has succeeded," but the lām was omitted because the speech became long, so its length became a substitute for it.

[Page 173 begins as the commentary continues.]

His exalted saying: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾. The exegetes mentioned three views regarding ḍuḥāhā (its brightness). Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: its light. Qatada said: it is the entire daytime, and this is the choice of al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba. Muqatil said: it is the heat of the sun.

The linguistic basis for this: al-Layth said: al-ḍaḥw is the rising of the day, and al-ḍuḥā is above that, and al-ḍaḥā (with a long vowel) means the day has extended and is near to midday. Abu al-Haytham said: al-ḍiḥ is the opposite of shade, and it is the light of the sun upon the face of the earth, and its origin is ḍuḥā. They found the ya' heavy with the ḥā' being sukūn, so they changed it and said ḍaḥḥ. Thus al-ḍuḥā is the sun's shining and its light; then the time at which the sun shines was named by it, as in His saying: ﴿except an evening or its forenoon﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 46]. So whoever among the exegetes said "in ḍuḥāhā, its light" is following the original meaning; likewise whoever said "it is the entire day," because all of the day is from the light of the sun. Whoever said "in al-ḍuḥā it is the heat of the sun" did so because its heat and its light are mutually connected: whenever its heat intensifies, its light intensifies, and vice versa. This is the weakest of the views.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, swore by the sun and its brightness only because of the great number of benefits connected to them. The people of knowledge were like the dead during the night; when the effect of dawn appeared in the east, this became like the Trumpet that blows the strength of life, and the dead became living. That life continues to increase, strengthen and perfect, and its utmost perfection occurs at the time of ḍaḥwa (the forenoon). This condition resembles the states of the Resurrection, and the time of ḍuḥā resembles the settling of the people of Paradise therein.

As for His saying: ﴿and by the moon when it follows it﴾, al-Layth said: talā yatlū means when it follows something. Regarding the moon being "following," there are several aspects:

First: the moon remains rising at the setting of the sun. This happens only in the first half of the month, when the sun sets and the moon then follows it in illumination. This is the view of Ata, from Ibn Abbas.

Second: when the sun sets, the moon follows it on the night of the crescent at sunset. This is the view of Qatada and al-Kalbi.

Third: al-Farra' said: the intended meaning of this following is that the moon takes its light from the sun. One says: "So-and-so follows so-and-so in such-and-such," meaning he takes from him.

Fourth: al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes round and complete, so it is as though it follows the sun in brightness and light, meaning when its light is complete and it stands in place of the sun in giving light, and that is on the bright nights.

Fifth: it follows it in the size of its body as perceived by the senses, and in the connection of the benefits of this world with its movement. In the science of the stars (ilm al-nujum) it has become clear that between them there is a relationship that does not exist between the sun and anything else.

As for His saying: ﴿and by the moon when it follows it﴾, al-Layth said: talā yatlū means when it follows something. Regarding the moon being "following," there are several aspects:

First: the moon remains rising at the setting of the sun. This happens only in the first half of the month, when the sun sets and the moon then follows it in illumination. This is the view of Ata, from Ibn Abbas.

Second: when the sun sets, the moon follows it on the night of the crescent at sunset. This is the view of Qatada and al-Kalbi.

Third: al-Farra' said: the intended meaning of this following is that the moon takes its light from the sun. One says: "So-and-so follows so-and-so in such-and-such," meaning he takes from him.

Fourth: al-Zajjaj said: it follows it when it becomes round and complete, so it is as though it follows the sun in brightness and light, meaning when its light is complete and it stands in place of the sun in giving light, and that is on the bright nights.

Fifth: it follows it in the size of its body as perceived by the senses, and in the connection of the benefits of this world with its movement. In the science of the stars (ilm al-nujum) it has become clear that between them there is a relationship that does not exist between the sun and anything else.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 91, verse 5:

God's statement: ﴿By the day when it reveals her﴾. The meaning of *tajliyah* (manifestation, unveiling) is making apparent and uncovering. To what does the pronoun in *jallaha* ("it reveals her") refer? There are two opinions.

The first, which is the view of al-Zajjaj, is that it refers to the sun. This is because "the day" is an expression for the light of the sun. Thus, whenever the day is more manifest, the sun is more manifest, since the strength and perfection of an effect indicate the strength of its cause. So the day brings the sun forth and makes it appear, as in God's statement: ﴿None but He will reveal it at its time﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], meaning, none but He will bring it out.

The second, which is the view of the majority, is that it refers to the darkness, or to the world, or to the earth, even though no mention of it has preceded. They say: "It became cold" (asbahat barida), meaning the morning, and "it sent down" (arsalat), meaning the sky.

God's statement: ﴿By the night when it covers her﴾. This means the night covers the sun and removes its light. This verse strengthens the first opinion regarding the verse before it, in two respects.

The first: since He made the night cover the sun and remove its light, it is apt to say "the day reveals her," in contrast to what was mentioned about the night.

The second: the pronoun in *yaghshaha* ("it covers her") refers to the sun without any disagreement. Therefore, in *jallaha* too it must refer to the sun, so that the pronouns in the rhyming clauses from the beginning of the surah up to here all refer to the sun. Al-Qaffal said: These four oaths are, in reality, only about the sun, but according to four attributes:

The first is the light that arises from it at the height of the day, which is the time when the spreading of living creatures and the bustle of people for their livelihood are complete. Among them is the moon's following of it and its taking light from it. Among them is the completion of its rising and its appearing with the coming of the day. Among them is the existence of the opposite of that with the coming of the night. Whoever reflects a little on the greatness of the sun, and then witnesses with the eye of his intellect in it the traces of being created and made, namely its finite measure and its composition from parts, passes from that to the greatness of its Creator. Glory be to Him, how great is His majesty!

﴿And by the sky and He who built it﴾.

Regarding this there are questions.

The first question: what Sahib al-Kashshaf mentioned, that if *ma* here were a verbal noun (masdariyyah), then the conjunction of ﴿fa-alhamaha﴾ ("then He inspired it") to it would truly cause corruption of the structure, and what the al-Qadi mentioned, that if this were an oath by the Creator of the sky, it would not be permissible to delay it past the mention of the sun. This is a good objection. What comes to my mind in answering it is this: the greatest of perceptible things is the sun, so He mentioned it together with its four attributes that indicate its greatness. Then, after that, He mentioned His holy essence and described it with three attributes, which are His governing of the sky and the earth and of composite things. He drew attention to composite things by mentioning the noblest of them, which is the soul. The purpose of this order is that intellect and sense should agree on the greatness of the body of the sun, and then the simple intellect argues from the sun, indeed from all the celestial and terrestrial bodies and composite things, to the existence of an originator for them. At that point the intellect attains, here, the perception of God's majesty and greatness in the manner that befits Him, and sense does not dispute it. This was like a path to drawing the intellect from the lowland of the world of perceptible things up to the height of the world of lordship and the wilderness of the greatness of the Self-Sufficient (al-Samadiyyah). Glory be to the One whose wisdom is magnified and whose word is perfected.

The second question: what is the benefit of His saying: ﴿and the sky and He who built it﴾?

The answer: when He described the sun with the four attributes that indicate its greatness, He followed this with an explanation of what indicates its createdness and the createdness of all celestial bodies. So He drew attention, through this verse, to that indication. This is because the sun and the sky are finite, and everything finite is specific to a determined measure, while it was possible in the intellect that there exist something greater than it and something smaller than it. Therefore the specification of the sun and all the celestial bodies with a determined measure must be due to the determination of a determiner and the governance of a governor. Just as the builder of a house builds it according to his will, so too the governor of the sun and all celestial bodies determines their measure according to His will. So His saying ﴿and He who built it﴾ is like an alert to this subtle point, which indicates the createdness of the sun and all celestial bodies.

The third question: why did He say ﴿and He who built it﴾ and not "and the One who built it" (man banaha)?

The answer has two aspects.

The first: the intention is to indicate the descriptive quality, as if it were said: "and the sky, and that great, powerful thing that built it, and the soul, and the Wise, the one utterly perfect in wisdom, who proportioned it."

The second: *ma* is used in the place of *man*, as in His statement: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ [al-Nisa: 22]. The reliance is on the first.

The fourth question: why did He mention these three things in defining the essence of God Most High, namely the sky, the earth, and the soul?

The answer: because inference about the absent (al-ghA'ib) is possible only through the present (al-shahid), and the present is nothing but the corporeal world. It has two kinds: simple and composite. The simple has two kinds: the upper, to which He alludes with His saying ﴿and the sky﴾, and the lower, to which He alludes with His saying ﴿and the earth﴾. The composite has several kinds, and the noblest of them is the beings that are souls, to which He alludes with His saying ﴿and the soul and He who proportioned it﴾.

[Page 174]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 91, verses 6–7:

As for His saying, ﴿And the earth and He who spread it out﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: Why did He place this after His saying, ﴿And the heaven and He who built it﴾? (It is because of His saying elsewhere, ﴿And the earth, after that, He spread it out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30].)

The second issue: Al-Layth said: al-tahw (ṭaḥw) is like al-dahw (daḥw), which means spreading out, and substituting the ṭā' for the dāl is permissible. The meaning is: He expanded it. ʿAṭā' and al-Kalbi said: He spread it out over the water.

As for His saying, ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾: if we take the soul (nafs) to mean the body, then its proportioning is the balancing of its limbs in accordance with what anatomy (ʿilm al-tashrīḥ) testifies to. If we take it to mean the governing faculty, then its proportioning is the granting to it of its many faculties, such as the faculty of hearing, the faculty of sight, the imaginative faculty, the cogitative faculty and the faculty of memory, in accordance with what the science of the soul (ʿilm al-nafs) testifies to. If it is asked: Why is "soul" indefinite (nakkarat)? We say: there are two aspects to this.

The first: that He intends by it a particular soul among souls, namely the holy prophetic soul (al-nafs al-qudsiyya al-nabawiyya). This is because every multiplicity must have in it one that is the chief: compound things form a genus under which are species, and their chief is the animal; the animal is a genus under which are species, and its chief is the human; the human has kinds and categories, and its chief is the Prophet. The prophets were many, so there must be one who is the absolute chief. Thus His saying, ﴿and a soul﴾, points to that soul which is the chief of the world of compounds by essential headship.

The second: that He intends every soul, and the purpose of the indefiniteness is multiplication in the manner mentioned in His saying, ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾ [al-Takwir: 14]. This is because animals are kinds whose number none can count except God, as He said after mentioning some animals: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 8]. Each kind has a particular soul distinguished from all others by the constituent differentia of its quiddity and the necessary properties that follow from that differentia. Who, then, can have his intellect encompass even a few of the properties of the soul of the gnat and the mosquito, let alone plunge into the seas of the secrets of God, glorified is He?

Regarding His saying, ﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾, the meaning derived from it has two possibilities.

The first: the inspiration (*ilham*) of wickedness and righteousness is making them understood and comprehended, and that one of them is good and the other evil, and that He enables it to choose whichever of them it wills. This is like His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. This interpretation accords with the doctrines of the Mu'tazilah (the Rationalist school), who said: "What indicates this is His saying after that: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it﴾." This view is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and from a group of the great exegetes (*mufassirun*).

The second possibility: He inspired the believing, God-fearing person with his God-consciousness, and inspired the disbeliever with his wickedness. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "He imposed on it its wickedness and its God-consciousness." Ibn Zayd said: "He placed that in it by His granting it success toward God-consciousness and His abandoning it to wickedness." Al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi preferred this. Al-Wahidi said: "Teaching, informing and clarifying are one thing, and inspiration (*ilham*) is another, for inspiration is that God places something in the heart of the servant, and when He places something in his heart, He has imposed it upon him. The root meaning of *ilham* comes from their saying *lahima al-shay'* and *iltahamahu* when one swallows it, and *alhamtuhu dhalika al-shay'* meaning 'I made that thing reach him.' This is the root meaning; then it was used for what God casts into the heart of the servant, because it is like making something reach (him). Therefore the interpretation that agrees with this root is the statement of Ibn Zayd, and it is explicit that God created in the believer his God-consciousness and in the disbeliever his wickedness. As for holding to His saying ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾, it is weak, because what is transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', Ikrimah, Muqatil and al-Kalbi is that the meaning is: 'Successful and happy is the soul that God purified, reformed and cleansed, and the meaning is that He enabled it to obey.'" This is the end of al-Wahidi's words, and it is complete.

I say: We have mentioned that the three verses were cited to show that He, glory be to Him, is the one who governs the upper and lower bodies, the simple and the composite. Thus nothing remains in the world of the sensible except that it has been established, by the implication of that admonition, that it occurs by His creation and governance. One thing remains that troubles the heart: whether it too is by His decree and destiny, namely the voluntary animal actions. So He, glory be to Him, drew attention, by His saying ﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾, to the fact that this also is from Him, through Him, and by His decree and destiny. At that point it is established that everything other than God occurs by His decree and destiny, and falls under His origination and His control.

Furthermore, what rationally indicates that the intended meaning of ﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ is abandonment and granting of success is what we have mentioned many times: voluntary actions depend on the occurrence of choices. If the occurrence of those choices is not from any agent, then the originated thing (*muhdath*) has dispensed with an agent, and this entails denying the Creator. If it is from an agent who is the servant, then *tasalsul* (an infinite regress) follows. If it is from God, then that is what is intended. Also, let the rational person test himself: a person is often unaware of something, then its image falls into his heart suddenly, and upon that image falling into the heart, an inclination toward it follows, and upon that inclination the movement of the limbs and the performance of the act follows. This establishes with certainty that the intended meaning of ﴿So He inspired it﴾ is what we have mentioned, not what the Mu'tazilah mentioned.

[p. 176]

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾, know that *tazkiyah* (purification or growth) is an expression for either purification or development. There are two opinions on the verse:

First: he has attained his goal who purifies his soul by cleansing it of sins through performing acts of obedience and avoiding acts of disobedience.

[p. 176]

Second: ﴿he has succeeded whom God purifies﴾. The judge (al-Qadi) accepted this interpretation and said: what is meant is that God decreed its purification and named it so, as people say in common usage, "So-and-so purifies so-and-so." Then he said: the first interpretation is closer, because the mention of the soul (*nafs*) has preceded explicitly, so returning the pronoun to it is more appropriate than returning it to something that is only implicitly mentioned.

Know that we have demonstrated by a decisive proof that what is meant by *alhamaha* (inspired it) is what we have mentioned, so the wording must be understood accordingly. As for his claim that this is to be understood as judgment and naming, it is weak, because the construction of the *tafʻīl* forms is based on creation (*takwīn*). Moreover, even if we grant that, what God has decreed cannot change, because a change in what is decreed would entail a change of the judgment from truth to falsehood and a change of knowledge into ignorance, and that is impossible, and what leads to an impossibility is itself impossible. As for his statement that the mention of the soul has already preceded, we say: the opposite is more appropriate, for the people of the language agree that returning a pronoun to the nearer antecedent is preferable to returning it to the more distant one. Moreover, His words ﴿so He inspired it﴾ are closer to the word *ma* (what) in it than to ﴿a soul﴾. Therefore, the preference lies with what we have mentioned. Among the things that confirm this interpretation is what al-Wahidi related in *al-Basit* from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pause when he recited ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ and say: "O God, grant my soul its piety, You are its Guardian and its Lord, and purify it, for You are the best of those who purify."

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and he has failed who corrupts it﴾. They said: *dassaha* (corrupts it) originally is *dassasa* (from *tadsis*), which means concealing one thing within another. So one of the two identical letters (the *sin*) was changed into a *yā'*, and the root of *dassā* is *dassasa*, just as the root of *taqaḍḍā* (for the falcon, meaning it swooped) is *taqaḍḍaḍa*, and as they said *alabbaytu* (I answered the call), whose root is *labbabtu*, and *mulabbī* (one who answers), whose root is *mulabbib*. Then we say: as for the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that emphasizes divine justice and human free will), they mentioned aspects that agree with their position:

The first: the people of righteousness make themselves manifest, while the people of wickedness conceal themselves and hide in hidden places, just as the generous among the Arabs settle on high ground so that their places become known and the needy come to them, and they light fires at night for travelers, whereas the miserly conceal their dwellings from those who seek them.

The second: ﴿he has failed who corrupts it﴾, that is, who inserts himself among the righteous while not being one of them.

The third: ﴿who corrupts it﴾ in sins, until he is immersed in them.

The fourth: ﴿who corrupts it﴾ means who instills wickedness into his soul, and that is due to his persistence in it and his association with its people.

The fifth: whoever turns away from acts of obedience and occupies himself with sins becomes obscure, abandoned, and forgotten, so he becomes like a hidden thing in concealment and obscurity.

As for our companions (the Ash'arites), they said: the meaning is that the soul has failed and lost, which God has led astray, misguided, made wicked, nullified, and destroyed. These are their words in explaining ﴿corrupts it﴾. Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: It is as if He, glorified is He, swore by the most noble of His creatures to the success of the one whom He purified and the loss of the one whom He forsook, so that no one would think that it is the person himself who undertakes the purification of his soul or its destruction through disobedience without a prior decree and a preceding destiny.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 91, verse 11–12:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thamud denied in their rebellion﴾, al-Farra' said: "Al-tughyan (transgression) and al-tughwa are both verbal nouns (masdar), except that al-tughwa fits better with the endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayat), so it was chosen for that reason. It is like al-da'wa from al-du'a'." Regarding the exegesis, there are two views:

The first: they committed the denial by means of their transgression, as you say, "He wronged me with his audacity against Allah, Exalted is He." The meaning is that their transgression led them to deny Him. This is the well-known view.

The second: al-tughwa is a name for their punishment by which they were destroyed. The meaning is "they denied their punishment," that is, they did not believe their messenger regarding the punishment he warned them of. This is not far-fetched, because the meaning of tughyan in the language is going beyond the usual measure. So it is permissible that the punishment that came upon them be called tughwa, because it was a cry (sayha) exceeding the usual measure. Or the implied meaning is: "they denied what they were threatened with of the punishment that is tughwa (overwhelming)." This interpretation is supported by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity﴾ [al-Haqqah: 4], that is, the punishment that befell them. Then He said: ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the Overwhelming Blast﴾ [al-Haqqah: 5], so He named the punishment by which they were destroyed "al-tagiyah" (the overwhelming).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When the most wretched of them was dispatched﴾. Inba'atha is the reflexive (muta'awi') of ba'atha. It is said: "I dispatched so-and-so to the matter, and he was dispatched for it." The meaning is that Thamud denied, due to their transgression, when the most wretched of them was dispatched, and he is the one who hamstrung the she-camel. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: he is a specific individual named Qudar ibn Salif, and he is used as a proverb: "More ill-omened than Qudar." He is the most wretched of the first people according to the ruling of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second: it is permissible that they were a group. It came in the singular form because of the rule for the superlative (af'al al-tafdil) when it is added (to a noun): between the singular and the plural, and the masculine and the feminine, you say: "These two are the best of people," and "These are the best of them." This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿But they denied him and hamstrung her﴾. It would also have been permissible to say "ashqawuha" (the most wretched of them), just as one says "afadiluhum" (their best).

The first: he is a specific individual named Qudar ibn Salif, and he is used as a proverb: "More ill-omened than Qudar." He is the most wretched of the first people according to the ruling of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second: it is permissible that they were a group. It came in the singular form because of the rule for the superlative (af'al al-tafdil) when it is added (to a noun): between the singular and the plural, and the masculine and the feminine, you say: "These two are the best of people," and "These are the best of them." This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿But they denied him and hamstrung her﴾. It would also have been permissible to say "ashqawuha" (the most wretched of them), just as one says "afadiluhum" (their best).

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 91, verses 13–14:

Regarding His saying, ﴿So the Messenger of Allah said to them: "The she-camel of Allah, and her drinking"﴾, there are several issues (masʾalah).

The first issue: The "Messenger" here is Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him. ﴿The she-camel of Allah﴾ means that he pointed to her when they resolved to hamstring her and he learned of what they had determined upon. He said to them: She is the she-camel of Allah and His sign, indicating His oneness and my prophethood. So beware of harming her, and beware also of preventing her from her water. We have explained in several places in this book that she had a day of drinking, and they had a day of drinking, and their livestock had a day of drinking. They were harmed by this in the matter of their livestock, so they resolved to hamstring her. Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him, warned them from time to time of a punishment that would descend upon them if they went ahead with it, and this condition was imagined in their minds. So he limited himself to saying to them: ﴿The she-camel of Allah and her drinking﴾, because this indication is sufficient together with the preceding matters that we have mentioned.

The second issue: ﴿The she-camel of Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a warning, like your saying: "The lion, the lion!" and "The boy, the boy!", with the verb "beware" (dharū) understood: "Leave her hamstringing alone, and beware of her drinking. So do not prevent her from it, and do not monopolize it to the exclusion of her."

Then Almighty God explained that the people did not refrain from denying Ṣāliḥ, or from hamstringing the she-camel, because of the punishment with which God Almighty had warned them. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿So they denied him and hamstrung her﴾. Then it is permissible that the one who actually did the hamstringing was one person, namely Qudār, and the act is attributed to him by direct agency, as He said: ﴿So he called his companion, and he took (the sword) and hamstrung her﴾ [al-Qamar: 29]. And the act may be attributed to the group because they were pleased with what that one person did. Qatādah said: It has been related to us that he refused to hamstring her until their young and old, their males and their females, pledged allegiance to him. This is the view of most of the exegetes. Al-Farrāʾ said: It has been said that they were two.

As for His saying: ﴿So their Lord crushed them down for their sin and leveled them﴾, know that there are several interpretations of "damdama" (crushed down):

The first: al-Zajjāj said: The meaning of "damdama" is that He closed the punishment over them. It is said: "I damdamtu upon the thing" when you close over it, and it is said: "a she-camel madmūmah," meaning one whose fat has been wrapped around her. When you repeat the closing, you say: "damdamtu ʿalayhi." Al-Wāḥidī said: "Ad-damm" in the language means smearing, and it is said of a fat thing: "as if it were smeared with fat, a smearing." So al-Zajjāj took "damdama" from this root in its intensive form, like "kubkibū" and its pattern. On this view, the meaning of "damdama ʿalayhim" is that He closed the punishment over them and encompassed them, like a thing that is smeared on from all sides.

The second: You say of a thing that is buried: "damdamtu ʿalayhi," meaning: I leveled it over him. So it is possible that the meaning of "damdama ʿalayhim" is that He leveled the earth over them, by destroying them and placing them under the dust.

The third: Ibn al-Anbārī said: "Damdama" means he became angry, and "ad-damdamah" is the speech that disturbs a man.

The fourth: "Damdama ʿalayhim" means He shook the earth with them. This was related by Thaʿlab from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, and it is the view of al-Farrāʾ.

As for His saying: ﴿and leveled them﴾, it allows two interpretations. For if we interpret "damdamah" as closing over and generality, then the meaning of "fa-sawwā" is that He leveled the damdamah over them and encompassed them with it, because their destruction was by the Cry of Jibrīl, peace be upon him, and that Cry destroyed them all, so it leveled over their young and old. And if we interpret it as "leveling," then the meaning is that He leveled the earth over them.

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾, there are several opinions.

The first: it is a reference (kinayah) to the Lord, the Exalted, since He is the nearest of those mentioned. Then they differed. Some said: He does not fear any consequence (tabi'ah) in the outcome, since al-'uqba and al-'aqibah are the same. It is as if He made clear that the Exalted acts thus in truth, and whatever He does that is wisdom and truth, He does not fear the consequence of His act. Others said: this was mentioned not to establish a literal fact but as a belittling of this deed, meaning: it is too insignificant for a consequence to be feared from it. God, the Exalted, is far above being described with this. Among them were those who said: the intent is to alert to the fact that He is thorough in punishment, for every king who fears a consequence guards himself to some degree, while God, the Exalted, since He fears none of the consequences, therefore He guards against nothing.

The second: it is a reference (kinayah) to the righteous one (salih), who is the Messenger. That is: the righteous one does not fear the outcome of this punishment that descends upon them. This is like a promise of his support and the repelling of hardships from him, should anyone try to harm him on account of that.

The third: the intent is that this most wretched one, who was the little red one of Thamud (ahmar Thamud), in what he undertook of slaughtering the she-camel, ﴿and he does not fear its consequence﴾. This verse, although it comes later, is according to this interpretation in the ruling of what precedes, as if it said: "When the most wretched of them was sent forth, and he does not fear its consequence." The meaning is that he proceeded to hamstring her while he was as one secure from the descent of destruction upon him and his people, so this act, alongside intense fear, is the act of one who does not fear at all, and for this he was attributed to ignorance and foolishness. In the recitation of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "wa-lam yakhaf" (and he did not fear), and in the codices of the people of Madinah and Syria: "fa-la yakhaf" (so he does not fear). And God knows best.

It is narrated that when Salih promised them the punishment after three days, the nine men who hamstrung the she-camel said: "Come, let us kill Salih. If he is truthful, we will hasten him before us, and if he is lying, we will join him to his she-camel." They came to him to ambush him by night, but the angels struck them with stones, and when they were delayed from their companions, they came to the dwelling of Salih and found them crushed by stones. They said to Salih: "You killed them." Then they resolved to attack him, but his clan stood between him and them, wearing weapons, and said to them: "By God, you will not kill him. He has promised you that the punishment will descend upon you within three days. If he is truthful, you will only increase your Lord's anger, and if he is lying, you are in front of what you intend." So they dispersed from him that night, and in the morning their faces were yellowed, and they became certain of the punishment. They sought Salih to kill him, but Salih fled and took refuge with the chief of one of the branches of Thamud, who was a polytheist, and he hid him from them, so they could not reach him. Then the punishment that befell them diverted them from him. This is His saying: ﴿and he does not fear its consequence﴾. And God knows best. May God send blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions.
